newsitem.title: UK: Mark crosses stick to tight ranges in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Mark crosses stick to tight ranges in late Europe.

text.p: The mark held steady against its crosses in afternoon European trade, weathering news of a German 1997 tax revenue shortfall and taking dollar volatility in its stride.
The mark ticked up from earlier lows by late trade but fairly narrow ranges prevailed and dealers said mark cross activity was fairly light.

"The main event was the German tax forecast but this came in as expected and made very little impact," said a U.S. bank dealer. "The talk of the Bundesbank revaluing assets seems more of a red herring, it's something that is probably long overdue but you can't say its pure coincidence."

The German Finance Ministry estimated 1997 tax revenues to be 18 billion marks below previous expectations, which analysts said would see Germany's budget deficit to GDP ratio up to 3.1-3.3 percent, above the 3.0 percent threshold of Europe's monetary union criteria.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel earlier today continued to call for strict interpretation of the EMU criteria and said later that Germany's chances of joining the single currency were unchanged despite the tax revenue shortfall. Waigel said Wednesday that further budgetary measures will be considered to meet EMU targets.

The prospect of Germany missing the criteria raises the risk of a delay to the EMU project and is seen as mark positive. But analysts say market sentiment has opted for a flexible interpretation of the criteria, leading to a broad-based, timely EMU start, lending support to the mark satellites.
"I think Germany can live with 3.2 or 3.3 percent, it's becoming clear from what German politicians are saying they want it to start on time," said Jesper Dannesboe, economist at ABN-Amro in London.
"We've already seen huge convergence in European markets, a delay would be quite explosive."

The Bundesbank today met Finance Minister Waigel, who presented potential changes to the central bank's accounting methods. This stirred speculation Waigel was seeking to boost funds for the government's budget by proposing a revaluation of Bundesbank assets, particularly gold, currently valued well below market value.

But analysts were sceptical such measures would have any impact on Germany's 1997 deficit, saying they would only have an impact next year and then only on Germany's debt level. In the case of gold, EU rules state a nation cannot reduce its deficit through central bank gold sales.
A short statement from the Bundesbank presented the plans as efforts to put the central bank's books in order ahead of EMU.
Mark/lira firmed slightly from early lows but the lira still looked well supported, mainly on EMU optimism and the prospect of a near-term cut in Italian interest rates.

This week's low inflation data for Spain and Portugal have reinforced this view, but analysts said the Bank of Italy may choose to wait for the presentation of the government's three-year economic plan due at the end of this month and the outcome of French elections before deciding on a rate move.
Mark/lira was trading at 986.80/7.30 at 1555 GMT versus 984.75/5.25 in late Europe on Wednesday.

The mark was slightly firmer against the French franc, trading at 3.3691/96 against 3.3677/80 late Wednesday. The latest French opinion polls continue to show the ruling centre-right in the lead ahead of the May 25/June 1 parliamentary election.

Mark/peseta was easier, with Wednesday's low inflation data reinforcing expectations of a Spanish repo rate cut as early as Friday. Activity was muted, however, by today's holiday in Spain. Mark/peseta was at 84.37/40 versus 84.41/42 Wednesday.
Mark/escudo bucked the trend, touching its highs for the year in early trade but settling back to 100.82/85 in late trade. It stood at 100.56/59 Wednesday.
Dealers said Portugal's growing chances of first-wave EMU participation could see the escudo gravitate towards its ERM central rate of 102.50 per mark.
"The perception is that ERM central rates are likely to be the basis for currency conversion into the euro," said the U.S. bank dealer.
-- Andrew Reierson, London Newsroom +44 171 542 6745
